extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of the State of New York and other voters considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Persuasive political essays (Federalist Papers Nos. 12–15) arguing for adoption of the proposed U.S. Constitution by demonstrating practical benefits of a national government in revenue, economy, defense, and administration, and answering objections about extent and expense. Targets objections about taxes, collection, representation distances, and the insufficiency of the Confederation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue primarily from indirect taxes (imposts/excises)
rubrics_metrics.description: National revenue in America must for a long time depend chiefly on duties, imposts, and excises (indirect taxes) rather than direct taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text emphasizes duties on imported articles as the principal branch of revenue; gives example that ardent spirits, at a shilling per gallon on an estimated four million gallons imported, could yield substantial funds. Notes that direct taxes and excises are politically impracticable in many parts of America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of extensive direct taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impracticable to raise very considerable sums by direct taxation in the U.S.; tax laws and new collection methods have repeatedly failed and treasuries remain empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains popular government and scarcity of money defeat extensive direct taxation; personal property is difficult to trace and tax; excise laws would be resisted by farmers and be unpopular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union enables more productive and higher duties without harming trade
rubrics_metrics.description: A general Union permits the same rate of duties to be more productive and makes it possible to increase rates without prejudice to trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform regulation under one government simplifies collection; central control reduces incentives for states to compete via low duties; federal regulation could raise duties (example: potentially trebling current averages) while maintaining trade health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and efficacy of customs collection under a single government
rubrics_metrics.description: With one government there is but one line to guard (the Atlantic coast), making prevention of smuggling and enforcement of customs simpler, cheaper, and more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts dispersed internal frontiers under disunion (which would require many patrols) with a single coast to guard; suggests a few armed vessels at port entrances and coordinated measures would suffice to prevent material infractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of illicit trade requires unified enforcement, not low duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate States, because of geography and familiar intercourse, would be driven by mutual jealousy to keep duties low to avoid illicit trade, undermining revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to rivers, bays, affinity of language/manners and inland communications as making inter-state contraband easy; France's extensive patrols are cited as an illustration of the difficulty of preventing inland smuggling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in government through a single national civil list
rubrics_metrics.description: Union produces economy by requiring only one national civil list for principal departments instead of multiple overlapping civil lists from several confederacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues separation into confederacies would multiply expensive national administrations; combined with required patrols and military establishments, disunion would be costlier than a single national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of duplicated administrative and military establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple governments would necessitate separate expenditures for inland patrols, military establishments, and civil lists, eroding any supposed savings from smaller governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that guarding inland communication and recurring military costs from jealous confederacies would nullify expense objections to the proposed plan; uses comparisons to Britain and hypothetical confederacies equal in size to Great Britain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability of an extended republic via representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic (distinct from a democracy) may be extended over a large region because the people govern by representatives who assemble and administer the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the natural limit of a republic is the distance allowing representatives to meet as often as necessary; offers geographic distance comparisons (e.g., U.S. distances vs. Britain/Germany) to show feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited federal jurisdiction with active subordinate governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The general government’s jurisdiction should be limited to enumerated objects affecting all states, while subordinate state governments retain authority over local matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that federal power will not absorb all lawmaking; local governments will retain responsibility for matters separable from national concerns, mitigating fears of an overbearing central government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union helps frontier states despite distance inconveniences
rubrics_metrics.description: Although remote states may have inconvenience in representation, they will benefit more from Union in defense and resources, maintaining equilibrium of advantages across the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues frontier states, being adjacent to foreign powers, stand to gain disproportionately in security and may accept representation inconveniences in exchange for protection and aid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must be capable of enforcing obligations and maintaining public credit
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient national government must be able to discharge engagements, pay debts, recover posts, possess troops and treasury, vindicate navigation rights, maintain public credit, and command respect abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses a litany of failures under the Confederation (debts unpaid, posts held by foreign powers, exclusion from Mississippi navigation, low commerce and depreciated land values) as indicators of insufficiency and the need for stronger national authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to legislate directly on individuals (not only states) is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The radical defect of the Confederation is legislation addressed to states as corporate entities rather than having authority to raise men and money by laws extending to individual citizens; effective government requires direct power over individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that requisitions on states are ineffectual in practice because the Union lacks power to compel individuals directly; argues that without direct authority the Union’s resolutions are mere recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform commercial regulations reduce opportunities for circuitous contraband
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the U.S. is distant from Europe, direct contraband is difficult, but circuitous contraband via one state through another would be easy unless regulations are uniform and enforced nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the difference between direct importation and indirect importation through neighboring states in small parcels makes national uniformity and enforcement necessary to preserve revenue and prevent smuggling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax policy can have beneficial social and economic side-effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain duties (e.g., higher duty on ardent spirits) could both raise revenue and promote agriculture, economy, morals, and health by reducing consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the spirits example to argue that higher duties may be sustainable and produce social benefits, not only fiscal ones.
